name: ต่อมลูกหมากอักเสบเรื้อรัง
pinyin: màn xìng qián liè xiàn yán
preview_text: ปัสสาวะที่แสบร้อนและเร่งด่วนของ Damp-Heat อาการปวดแสบปวดร้อนจากภาวะเลือดติดขัด และอาการปวดเย็นจากภาวะขาดหยางของไต เป็นอาการที่แตกต่างกัน 3 ประการใน TCM - การตอบสนองแต่ละครั้ง...
categories: ["ปัญหาทางเดินปัสสาวะและกระเพาะปัสสาวะ", "ปัญหาต่อมลูกหมาก"]
conventional_description: Chronic prostatitis (also called chronic pelvic pain syndrome) is defined as persistent pain or discomfort in the pelvic region, perineum, or genitals, often accompanied by urinary symptoms like frequency, urgency, or painful urination, lasting at least three months. It affects men of all ages and can significantly impact quality of life. Diagnosis is typically based on symptoms and a physical exam; urine and prostate fluid tests may rule out bacterial infection, but most cases are non-bacterial.
conventional_treatments: Standard treatment often includes a combination of antibiotics (if an infection is suspected), alpha-blockers to relax the bladder neck and improve urine flow, anti-inflammatory medications, and sometimes muscle relaxants. Pelvic floor physical therapy and stress management are also recommended. Because the exact cause is often unclear, treatment can be trial-and-error.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, the prostate is understood as part of the ‘jing chamber’ (精室), a system intimately connected to the Kidneys, which store the body’s essential energy and govern the lower orifices including urination and reproduction. When Kidney function is weak - whether from overwork, aging, or chronic illness - the prostate area becomes vulnerable to invasion by external pathogens like Dampness and Heat, or to internal stagnation.
The Liver channel physically runs through the lower abdomen and wraps around the genitals. Emotional stress, frustration, or a sedentary lifestyle can cause Liver Qi to stagnate, creating a sense of distension, pain, and urinary difficulty. This is why chronic prostatitis often flares up during periods of tension or after long hours of sitting.
Diet plays a major role too. Overconsumption of greasy, spicy, or alcohol-rich foods generates internal Damp-Heat, which sinks downward and clogs the lower burner. This leads to the classic symptoms of burning, urgent urination with cloudy yellow urine and a heavy sensation in the groin - the Damp-Heat pattern. If not cleared, this Damp-Heat can congeal and obstruct the flow of Qi and Blood, causing fixed, stabbing pain.
Over time, chronic inflammation can deplete the body’s reserves, leading to deficiency patterns. Kidney Yin Deficiency creates a dry, hot state with night sweats and a red tongue, while Kidney Yang Deficiency leaves the area cold and aching with frequent nighttime urination. A TCM practitioner will look at your whole picture - tongue, pulse, emotional state, and the exact nature of your pain - to determine which pattern or combination of patterns is at play.
classical_translation: "When the bladder is obstructed, it causes painful, dribbling urination (癃, long); when it fails to restrain, it causes incontinence. This early principle links lower burner dysfunction to both obstruction and weakness, which underpin chronic prostatitis patterns."
classical_source:
Huang Di Nei Jing (Su Wen)  ,  Chapter 23, Xuan Ming Wu Qi 									·

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by listening carefully to the story of your symptoms - when they started, what makes them better or worse, and how they feel day to day. The quality of urinary discomfort, the location and nature of pain, and your overall energy and mood are the first signposts that point toward one pattern rather than another.
If your main complaints are frequent, urgent, and burning urination with dark yellow urine, and you feel a heavy, damp sensation in the genital area, the pattern is likely Damp-Heat in the Lower Burner. The tongue coating will appear thick, yellow, and greasy, and the pulse feels slippery and rapid - signs of heat and moisture clogging the lower body.
When the dominant issue is fixed, stabbing, or distending pain in the perineum, lower abdomen, or lower back, and urination is dribbling or painful, Qi and Blood Stagnation is the key pattern. The tongue often looks dark or purplish with possible red spots, and the pulse may feel wiry or choppy, reflecting obstructed flow.
If your discomfort is closely tied to your emotional state - with a sense of fullness in the perineum, frequent sighing, chest tightness, and irritability or depression - Liver Qi Stagnation is the central pattern. The pulse is typically wiry, and the tongue may look normal or slightly dusky, pointing to constrained energy rather than heat or cold.
For those who feel more depleted than inflamed, with a deep soreness in the lower back and knees, dry mouth at night, and perhaps nocturnal emissions, Kidney Yin Deficiency is suspected. The tongue is red with little or no coating, and the pulse is thin and rapid, indicating a lack of cooling, nourishing fluids.
When fatigue, a constant feeling of cold, low libido, and weak erections dominate the picture, the practitioner looks for Kidney Yang Deficiency. The tongue is pale and puffy with a thin white coating, and the pulse is deep, slow, and weak - signs that the body’s warming fire is low.
Less often, if there is a distinct cold sensation and sharp pain along the groin and testicles, and the symptoms worsen with cold weather, Stagnation of Cold in the Liver Channel may be present. The tongue is pale with a white coating, and the pulse feels tight or wiry, as if the channel is being squeezed by cold.

patterns.symptoms: ["Burning or stinging during urination", "Frequent, urgent urination with small volume", "Cloudy or dark yellow urine", "Scrotal dampness or itching", "Heavy, dragging sensation in the legs and lower body", "Thirst with no desire to drink much"]
patterns.worse_with: Spicy or greasy food, Alcohol, Hot and humid weather, Prolonged sitting, Stress and frustration
patterns.better_with: Cool compress on perineum, Drinking plenty of water, Light diet with cooling foods, Urinating as soon as the urge arises, Gentle walking or stretching
patterns.why_this_happens: When Damp-Heat sinks into the lower burner, it settles in the pelvic region and congests the prostate. The Heat component stirs up inflammation, causing urinary urgency, burning, and dark yellow urine. The Dampness creates a heavy, dragging sensation in the groin and perineum, and leads to cloudy or sticky discharges. Together they obstruct the bladder's normal opening and closing, resulting in frequent, scanty urination.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Red body, slightly swollen, with a yellow greasy coating thickest at the root. Pulse: Slippery (滑 huá) and rapid (数 shuò), sometimes soggy (濡 rú), more pronounced at the rear (Chi) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Spicy, greasy, and alcoholic foods directly introduce Damp-Heat into the body, fueling the pattern. Hot, humid weather and prolonged sitting trap dampness in the lower body. Cooling foods and adequate hydration help drain the excess heat and dampness, while gentle movement keeps Qi and fluids flowing, preventing stagnation.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, greasy, and fried foods, as well as alcohol and coffee, which create Damp-Heat. Eat light, cooling foods like barley, mung beans, cucumber, and celery. Stay well hydrated to help flush the urinary tract. Avoid prolonged sitting, which stagnates Qi and Dampness in the pelvis.

patterns.better_with: Gentle exercise like walking or tai chi, Warm compress on lower abdomen, Stress reduction and relaxation, Avoiding prolonged sitting
patterns.why_this_happens: In chronic prostatitis, prolonged damp-heat, emotional frustration, or a sedentary lifestyle can cause Qi to stagnate and Blood to congeal in the lower burner. This blockage creates fixed, stabbing pain in the perineum, lower belly, and lower back, and it impairs the smooth flow of urine, leading to dribbling and stinging. The stasis also darkens the tongue and makes the pulse feel rough and tight.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: dark purple body with purple stasis spots, distended sublingual veins, thin white coat. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián) and choppy (涩 sè), like a taut string scraping bamboo.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Movement and warmth help disperse stagnant Qi and Blood, while stress and prolonged sitting tighten the Liver and block flow, directly aggravating the core stasis. Cold foods congeal Blood, and greasy or alcoholic items generate damp-heat that can further obstruct the channels.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warming, blood-moving foods like turmeric, ginger, cinnamon, and dark leafy greens. Avoid cold, raw foods and icy drinks, which can congeal Blood. Gentle daily movement - walking, stretching, tai chi - is essential to keep Qi and Blood flowing. Take breaks from sitting every hour. Manage stress with deep breathing or meditation, as emotional tension tightens the Liver and worsens stagnation.

patterns.better_with: Stress reduction and relaxation, Gentle exercise like walking or stretching, Warm baths, Avoiding alcohol and greasy food, Deep breathing exercises
patterns.why_this_happens: The Liver governs the smooth flow of Qi throughout the body. When emotional stress, frustration, or prolonged sitting block this flow, Qi stagnates in the pelvic region, causing the Liver channel to become congested. This leads to the characteristic perineal distension, lower abdominal bloating, and urinary discomfort seen in chronic prostatitis.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Normal or slightly dark body with red or purplish sides and a thin white coat. Pulse: Wiry (弦 xián), taut like a guitar string.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Stress and frustration directly cause Liver Qi to stagnate, which then congests the pelvic region because the Liver channel passes through the genital area. This stagnation leads to the distension, discomfort, and urinary symptoms. Relaxation and gentle movement help Qi flow freely, while alcohol and greasy foods create internal Dampness and Heat that further obstruct the Liver's function.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Manage stress with meditation, deep breathing, or gentle yoga. Avoid prolonged sitting; take short walks every hour. Limit alcohol, caffeine, and spicy foods, which can aggravate Qi stagnation. Include foods like peppermint tea, turmeric, and green leafy vegetables to gently move Qi.

patterns.symptoms: ["Soreness and weakness of the lower back and knees", "Night sweats", "Dry mouth and throat, especially at night", "Heat in the palms, soles, and chest (five-centre heat)", "Scanty, dark yellow urine without strong burning", "Nocturnal emissions or premature ejaculation", "Insomnia with vivid dreams"]
patterns.worse_with: Overwork and late nights, Spicy, fried, or heating foods, Excessive sexual activity, Emotional stress and frustration
patterns.better_with: Adequate rest and early nights, Cool, calm environment, Moistening foods (pears, black sesame)
patterns.why_this_happens: The Kidneys are the root of all Yin and govern the lower orifices, including urination and reproduction. When Kidney Yin is depleted by overwork, chronic illness, or excessive sexual activity, the body loses its cooling, moistening anchor. This generates empty Heat that rises and disturbs the lower burner, leading to a dry, undernourished prostate that cannot function smoothly. The result is a pattern of chronic, low-grade urinary discomfort, nocturnal emissions, and a persistent dull ache in the lower back and knees rather than the acute burning of Damp-Heat.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin, and dry with little or no coating, possible cracks. Pulse: fine (xi) and rapid (shu).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney Yin is a deep, cooling reserve that is easily drained by overwork, insufficient sleep, and excessive sexual activity. Spicy and heating foods add fuel to the empty fire that already simmers from Yin deficiency, while rest and moistening, cooling foods help to rebuild that reserve. Stress stirs up Liver Qi, which can transform into fire and further consume Yin, so calmness and gentle movement protect what little Yin remains.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Protect your Yin by going to bed early and avoiding overwork or late-night screen time. Favour moistening foods like black sesame, walnuts, goji berries, and pears. Reduce spicy, greasy, and fried foods, as well as alcohol and coffee, which dry out the body. Moderate sexual activity to preserve Kidney essence, and practice gentle exercises like tai chi or walking rather than exhausting workouts.

patterns.symptoms: ["Cold and aching lower back and knees", "Frequent, clear urination, especially at night", "Deep fatigue and low spirits", "Reduced libido or erectile dysfunction", "Aversion to cold, worse in the lower body", "Loose stools or early morning diarrhea"]
patterns.worse_with: Cold and damp environments, Overwork and exhaustion, Excessive sexual activity, Cold raw foods and drinks
patterns.better_with: Warmth on the lower back, Rest and avoiding overwork, Warm, cooked meals, Moxibustion on the lower abdomen
patterns.why_this_happens:
Kidney Yang is the body's warming, transformative fire. When it weakens, the lower burner loses its heat, and the prostate area becomes cold and sluggish. This leads to a persistent, dull ache in the lower back and perineum, frequent urination especially at night, and a marked drop in sexual vitality.
Without enough Yang, the body cannot properly move and transform fluids, so urine becomes frequent, clear, and copious. The deep fatigue and aversion to cold are signs that the inner fire is too low to energize the body or keep the channels warm.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, tender body with teeth marks and a wet white coating. Pulse: deep (沉 chén), slow (迟 chí), and weak, especially at the rear (Chi) positions.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney Yang is the body's inner fire, so cold environments and raw foods smother it, while warmth and moxibustion feed it. Overwork and excessive sexual activity drain the Kidneys' reserve of Yang, deepening the deficiency. Rest and nourishing, warm foods allow the body to conserve and slowly rebuild the fire, which is the essence of recovery in this pattern.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep the lower back and abdomen warm at all times. Eat warm, cooked foods like stews, soups, and root vegetables, and add gentle warming spices such as cinnamon, ginger, and fennel. Avoid raw, cold foods and icy drinks. Gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi supports Yang without exhausting it. Prioritize rest and avoid overwork, especially late nights and excessive sexual activity.

patterns.pattern_name: Stagnation of Cold in the Liver Channel
patterns.symptoms: ["Cold, cramping lower abdominal pain that pulls toward the groin or testicles", "Scrotal contraction or testicular cold pain", "Pain and discomfort worsen with cold exposure and improve with warmth", "Feeling of cold in the lower belly and cold limbs", "Pale tongue with a white, slippery coating"]
patterns.worse_with: Exposure to cold weather or drafts, Iced or cold foods and beverages, Prolonged sitting on cold surfaces, Emotional stress and frustration
patterns.better_with: Applying warmth (heating pad, warm bath), Warm drinks and cooked, spiced foods, Rest and lying down with knees drawn up, Gentle stretching or walking
patterns.why_this_happens: The Liver channel runs through the lower abdomen and wraps around the genitals. When Cold settles into this channel, it constricts the flow of Qi and Blood, causing a characteristic cold, cramping pain that can radiate from the lower belly into the perineum and testicles. This persistent tightness and poor circulation in the pelvic region can contribute to the chronic discomfort and urinary symptoms of prostatitis.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale body with a white, slippery coating, moist. Pulse: deep (Chen), wiry (Xian), and slow (Chi) or tight (Jin).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold has a constricting nature that freezes the flow of Qi and Blood in the Liver channel, directly causing the cramping pain. Warmth relaxes the channel, dilates the vessels, and restores circulation, which is why heat brings relief. Stress and frustration cause Qi to stagnate, which compounds the Cold-induced constriction and worsens the pain.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep the lower back and abdomen warm at all times; a warm compress or hot water bottle can bring immediate relief. Favor warm, cooked foods like soups, stews, and spices such as ginger, cinnamon, and fennel. Avoid cold drinks, raw foods, and sitting on cold surfaces for long periods. Gentle daily movement like walking or stretching helps keep Qi flowing.

The formula works by clearing internal Heat and promoting healthy urine flow to flush out the pathogenic factors.

It is commonly applied for hot, swollen, painful joints (especially in the knees and feet), lower limb weakness, and conditions like gout and eczema that involve a combination of inflammation and heavy, waterlogged tissue. The formula works by cooling inflammation, drying excess moisture, strengthening digestion to stop dampness at its source, and directing the formula's effects downward to the legs and lower body.

It is particularly well suited for women experiencing menstrual cramps, irregular periods, or fertility difficulties linked to Cold and Blood stasis in the pelvic area. The formula combines warming herbs with Blood-moving herbs to address both the underlying Cold and the resulting stagnation.

It works by smoothing the flow of Liver Qi, relieving tension, and gently moving blood to stop pain. It is one of the most widely used formulas for stress-related digestive and emotional complaints.

formulas.description: A classical formula that nourishes the body's cooling Yin fluids while clearing excess internal heat. It is commonly used for symptoms such as hot flashes, night sweats, tinnitus, sore throat, dry mouth, and low back aching that arise when the Kidneys become depleted and the body overheats from within. It builds on the famous Liu Wei Di Huang Wan (Six Ingredient Rehmannia Pill) with two additional cooling herbs.

formulas.description: A classical warming and tonifying formula designed to restore Kidney Yang, the body's foundational warmth and vitality. It is commonly used for people experiencing deep fatigue, persistent cold sensations, lower back weakness, reduced sexual function, or frequent urination due to depletion of the Kidney's warming capacity. The formula combines Yang-warming herbs with nourishing substances to rebuild vitality from within, following the principle that Yang is best restored by providing it with a nourishing Yin foundation.

It works by gently warming these organ systems, improving the flow of Qi, and stopping pain. It is commonly used for conditions like inguinal hernia, testicular pain, and cold-type menstrual cramps.

faqs.question: Can TCM really help with chronic prostatitis?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM can be very effective for chronic prostatitis, especially for the non-bacterial type that often doesn't respond well to antibiotics. By identifying the underlying pattern - whether it's Damp-Heat, Qi stagnation, or Kidney deficiency - a practitioner can tailor a treatment plan that addresses the root cause, not just the symptoms. Many men who haven't found relief with conventional treatments experience significant improvement with herbs and acupuncture.

faqs.question: How long does TCM treatment take to work?
faqs.answer: Most men notice some improvement within 2-4 weeks. For excess patterns like Damp-Heat or Liver Qi Stagnation, relief may come even faster. However, because chronic prostatitis often involves deeper imbalances, a full course of treatment usually lasts 3-6 months to ensure lasting results. Your practitioner will monitor your progress and adjust the formula as your pattern shifts.

faqs.question: Is acupuncture safe for prostate issues?
faqs.answer: Yes, acupuncture is safe when performed by a licensed professional. For chronic prostatitis, needles are typically placed on the lower abdomen, sacrum, and legs - points like Sanyinjiao (SP-6), Zhongji (REN-3), and Shenshu (BL-23) - to regulate the lower burner and relieve pain. Some men worry about needles near the genitals, but the points used are on the abdomen and back, not directly on the prostate. Mild soreness at the needle site is normal and temporary.

faqs.question: What dietary changes should I make while undergoing TCM treatment?
faqs.answer: Diet plays a crucial role in managing chronic prostatitis. Generally, avoid spicy, greasy, and deep-fried foods, alcohol, and excessive coffee - these generate Damp-Heat and can worsen burning and urgency. Favor cooling, hydrating foods like cucumber, watermelon, mung beans, and celery. If your pattern is more cold or deficient (e.g., Kidney Yang Deficiency), warm, cooked foods like soups and stews with ginger and cinnamon are better. Your TCM practitioner will give you specific dietary advice based on your pattern.

faqs.question: Can I combine TCM with my current medications like antibiotics or alpha-blockers?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM can usually be combined with conventional treatments like antibiotics, alpha-blockers, or anti-inflammatories. There are no known severe interactions, but you should always inform both your TCM practitioner and your medical doctor about all medications and supplements you are taking. If you are on blood thinners, mention this especially, as some herbs (like Dang Gui) can have mild blood-moving effects.

faqs.question: Will I need to take herbs forever?
faqs.answer: No, the goal of TCM is to correct the underlying imbalance so that your body can maintain health on its own. Once your symptoms have resolved and your pattern has shifted, the herbal formula will be adjusted and eventually tapered off. Some men with chronic, deep-seated deficiency may benefit from a low-dose maintenance formula for a few months after the main treatment, but long-term dependence is not the aim.

research.title: Acupuncture for chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome
research.description: Cochrane systematic review assessing acupuncture versus sham acupuncture or usual care. Moderate-quality evidence suggested acupuncture modestly reduces pain and improves quality of life with few adverse events.
research.periodical: Franco JV, Turk T, Jung JH, et al. Acupuncture for chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2018, Issue 5. Art. No.: CD012549.

research.title: Chinese herbal medicine for chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: Meta-analysis of 22 RCTs involving over 2,400 patients. Herbal medicine significantly improved NIH-CPSI total scores and pain subscores compared to placebo or antibiotics, with fewer side effects.
